title: The polymerase chain reaction copies DNA millions of times
summary: In 1983 Kary Mullis, a chemist at Cetus Corporation in Emeryville, California, conceived the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which copies a chosen stretch of DNA over and over. Developed by Mullis and Cetus colleagues and published from 1985, it became one of the most widely used techniques in biology and medicine.
explanation:
Studying a gene once meant working with tiny amounts of DNA by slow, difficult methods. Mullis's idea was to use two short primers flanking a target sequence and repeated cycles of heating and copying, so that the number of copies doubles with each cycle. Colleagues including Randall Saiki, Stephen Scharf, Fred Faloona and Henry Erlich generated the data that proved it worked, and the first paper using PCR, on diagnosing sickle-cell anaemia, appeared in Science in 1985.

In 1985–86 Cetus scientists replaced the original enzyme with Taq polymerase from a heat-loving bacterium, which survives the heating steps and allowed the process to be automated. Mullis shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

title: A robot arm guides a brain biopsy
summary: In 1985 Yik San Kwoh and colleagues at Memorial Medical Center in Long Beach, California, used an industrial PUMA robot arm, guided by CT scans, to position a needle for brain biopsies. It is generally regarded as the first use of a robot in surgery.
explanation:
In stereotactic brain surgery, instruments are guided to a target deep in the brain that the surgeon cannot see, using coordinates from scans. Kwoh, director of tomography research at Memorial Medical Center, linked a PUMA industrial robot arm to a minicomputer that used CT images to calculate the path to a lesion and hold the instrument at exactly the right angle, while surgeons pushed the probe in.

The robot was first used on 11 April 1985 and had been used in seven operations by December. The arm's manufacturer later refused to allow its use in surgery because it had been designed to work away from people, and the project stopped.

title: DNA fingerprinting identifies individuals
summary: On 10 September 1984 Alec Jeffreys at the University of Leicester saw that patterns of highly variable DNA sequences differed between individuals while showing family resemblances. explanation:
Jeffreys was studying how genes vary and evolve, using probes for repeated DNA sequences called minisatellites. When he developed an X-ray film showing DNA from members of a technician's family, he saw a pattern of bands unique to each person but shared in part between relatives.

He published in Nature in 1985. That year a lawyer asked him to help a Ghanaian-British boy threatened with deportation; DNA fingerprinting showed he was his mother's son and he was allowed to stay. The technique was soon used in paternity disputes and, from 1986–88, in the first criminal investigation solved by DNA, in Leicestershire.

title: Fluoxetine (Prozac) and the SSRI antidepressants
summary: Chemists at Eli Lilly identified fluoxetine in 1972 as a selective blocker of serotonin reuptake. Approved in the US as Prozac in December 1987, it became the best-selling antidepressant and changed how depression was treated and understood.
explanation:
Older tricyclic antidepressants carried risks including heart effects and were dangerous in overdose. At Lilly, Bryan Molloy and colleagues made dozens of compounds related to an antihistamine; David Wong proposed testing them for effects on the reuptake of serotonin, and in 1972 one compound, later named fluoxetine, proved the most potent and selective.

Development took more than 16 years. Fluoxetine was approved for depression by the US FDA on 29 December 1987 and quickly outsold its rivals, as doctors saw it as safer and better tolerated. By 2002 it had been prescribed to more than 40 million people.

title: Statins: from a Japanese mould to the most prescribed heart drugs
summary: In 1973 Akira Endo at Sankyo in Tokyo discovered compactin, a mould product that blocks the body's main cholesterol-making enzyme. Merck developed a related compound, lovastatin, which in 1987 became the first statin approved for use.
explanation:
Inspired by penicillin's origin in a mould, Endo screened thousands of fungal cultures for substances that inhibit HMG-CoA reductase. Compactin, from Penicillium citrinum, lowered cholesterol in dogs, rabbits and monkeys, and Endo and the physician Akira Yamamoto gave it to patients with extremely high cholesterol. Sankyo halted development after concerns about tumours in dogs given high doses.

Merck, whose scientists led by Alfred Alberts found lovastatin in another fungus, resumed trials after evidence of benefit and safety; the FDA approved lovastatin in 1987. Statins became among the most widely used drugs in the world for preventing heart attacks and strokes.

title: A balloon-expandable stent holds arteries open
summary: Julio Palmaz, an Argentine radiologist in San Antonio, Texas, invented a metal mesh tube that is expanded by a balloon inside a narrowed artery to prop it open. Patented in 1985, it was approved for leg arteries in 1991 and, as the Palmaz–Schatz stent, for coronary arteries in 1994.

title: Patricia Bath's laser probe for cataract surgery
summary: In 1986 the ophthalmologist Patricia Bath invented the Laserphaco Probe, which uses a laser to vaporise a cataract. Her 1988 patent made her the first African American woman physician to receive a US medical patent.

title: Testing IVF embryos for genetic disease before transfer
summary: In April 1990 Alan Handyside, Robert Winston and colleagues at Hammersmith Hospital, London, reported pregnancies after removing a single cell from early IVF embryos and testing it, so that only embryos free of a serious X-linked disease were transferred.

Couples at risk of passing on a serious genetic disease could previously only test a pregnancy and consider ending it. The Hammersmith team, building on IVF, removed one cell from embryos at the six-to-eight-cell stage, three days after fertilisation, and used the new technique of PCR to detect a Y-chromosome sequence. Because the families carried X-linked conditions such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy that affect boys, only female embryos were transferred.

title: Wearable pumps deliver insulin continuously
summary: Arnold Kadish built a backpack-sized insulin-delivery system in 1963, but practical wearable pumps came in the late 1970s. In 1978 John Pickup, Harry Keen and colleagues at Guy's Hospital, London, showed that a small battery-driven pump infusing insulin under the skin could achieve near-normal blood sugar.

title: Excimer lasers reshape the cornea: PRK and LASIK
summary: After IBM scientists showed in the early 1980s that an ultraviolet excimer laser could remove tissue precisely, Stephen Trokel proposed using it to reshape the cornea in 1983. explanation:
At IBM's Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, Rangaswamy Srinivasan, Samuel Blum and James Wynne found that excimer laser pulses could etch tissue with almost no heat damage. The New York ophthalmologist Stephen Trokel collaborated with them in 1983, experimenting on cow eyes and publishing the idea of sculpting the cornea to correct short sight.

Theo Seiler in Germany began excimer procedures on human eyes in 1987, and in 1988 Marguerite McDonald in the United States performed the first PRK, which removes the surface layer of the cornea, on a sighted short-sighted eye. Pallikaris's team at the University of Crete combined the laser with a hinged corneal flap, performing the first LASIK on a blind human eye in 1989. LASIK became the most common refractive operation.

title: Liposuction is developed in Rome and Paris
summary: In the mid-1970s the Italian father-and-son surgeons Arpad and Giorgio Fischer in Rome developed blunt hollow cannulas and suction to remove fat. In 1977 Yves-Gérard Illouz in Paris introduced the safer 'wet' technique, and liposuction became one of the most common cosmetic operations.
explanation:
The Fischers used a blunt tunnelling technique with suction, initially on the outer thighs, though some patients developed fluid leaks. Illouz and Pierre Fournier in Paris refined and popularised the method: Illouz's wet technique injected a salt solution into the fat before suction, reducing bleeding.

By 1987 the American dermatologist Jeffrey Klein had introduced the tumescent technique, a further refinement that became widely used.

whatChanged: Fat could be removed through small incisions rather than by open surgery with large scars.
whyItMattered: Liposuction became one of the most frequently performed cosmetic procedures, with uses also in reconstructive surgery and fat grafting.
limitations: Sources give 1974, 1975 or 1976 for the Fischers' first technique.
Early operations caused bleeding and other complications; safety improved only with later refinements.

title: Tissue engineering: growing tissue on biodegradable scaffolds
summary: From the mid-1980s the surgeon Joseph Vacanti of Boston Children's Hospital and the engineer Robert Langer of MIT seeded cells onto biodegradable polymer scaffolds and implanted them in animals. Their 1993 review in Science named and defined the field of tissue engineering.
explanation:
Organ transplantation was limited by the shortage of donors. Vacanti and Langer reasoned that cells could be grown on artificial scaffolds that the body would gradually absorb, forming new tissue. In a 1988 paper they reported attaching liver, intestinal and pancreatic cells to bioerodable polymers and implanting the cell–polymer scaffolds in animals.

The term 'tissue engineering' was formally defined at a US National Science Foundation meeting in 1987. Langer and Vacanti's 1993 review in Science brought the concept to a wide audience and framed most later work in the field.

limitations: Others, including Eugene Bell and Yuan-Cheng Fung, also shaped the early field.

title: Landsteiner discovers the human blood groups
summary: In 1901 Karl Landsteiner, at the University of Vienna's Institute of Pathological Anatomy, showed that serum from some healthy people clumps the red blood cells of others, and sorted human blood into groups later called A, B and O. The discovery made safe blood transfusion possible.
explanation:
Transfusions between people were dangerous and unpredictable, and the clumping of red cells when blood was mixed was generally put down to disease. In a footnote to a paper in 1900, Landsteiner noted that serum from healthy people clumped the red cells of other healthy people. In 1901 he published the evidence: the reaction came from antibodies in the serum acting on the cells, and it reflected normal differences between individuals.

He identified three groups, and in 1902 his colleagues Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli described a fourth, AB. In 1910 Emil von Dungern and Ludwik Hirszfeld proposed that blood groups are inherited, which led to their use in paternity cases. Landsteiner received the 1930 Nobel Prize.

people.name: Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli

whatChanged: The reactions that made many transfusions fatal could be explained, and later tested for before blood was given.
whyItMattered: Blood typing made transfusion a routine medical practice, underpinning modern surgery, trauma care and blood banks.
limitations: Leonard Landois had earlier described clumping when animal blood was mixed with human blood; Landsteiner showed that it also happened between humans.
Landsteiner described three groups; the fourth, AB, and the Rh system were found later.

title: Alzheimer links a patient's dementia to changes in her brain
summary: In 1901 the psychiatrist Alois Alzheimer began following Auguste Deter, a 51-year-old patient at the Frankfurt asylum with memory loss and confusion. After her death he examined her brain and, on 3 November 1906, described the plaques and tangles he found there. The condition was later named after him.
explanation:
Auguste Deter's family had noticed that she had become confused, forgetful and jealous, and often got lost. Alzheimer, who moved to Emil Kraepelin's laboratory in Munich, arranged to receive her brain when she died, in 1906.

Using a new silver stain, he found a shrunken brain containing fibre-like tangles inside nerve cells and deposits he called 'miliary foci', now known as amyloid plaques. He presented the case at the meeting of South-West German Psychiatrists in Tübingen on 3 November 1906, where it met with little interest, and published it in 1907. Kraepelin later named the condition after him.

whyItMattered: Alzheimer's disease is now recognised as the most common cause of dementia, and the plaques and tangles he described remain central to research on it.
limitations: For decades the name was used mainly for dementia beginning before old age.
The lecture met with little interest, and the disease was recognised only slowly.

title: Hopkins shows that food contains vital 'accessory factors'
summary: In a 1906 lecture Frederick Gowland Hopkins of Cambridge argued that diets need small amounts of unknown substances besides protein, fat and carbohydrate. His 1912 feeding experiments in rats showed it, helping found the study of vitamins.
explanation:
Physiologists assumed that a diet supplying enough protein, fat, carbohydrate and minerals was complete. In his 1906 address to the Society of Public Analysts, Hopkins suggested that diseases such as rickets and scurvy might be caused by a lack of other trace substances in food.

His experiments, begun in 1906–07 and published in the Journal of Physiology in 1912, fed young rats a purified diet. They stopped growing, but a tiny daily addition of milk, making up only a few per cent of the food eaten, restored normal growth. Hopkins shared the 1929 Nobel Prize with Christiaan Eijkman, whose work on beriberi had pointed in the same direction.

whyItMattered: The idea led to the identification of the vitamins and to the prevention of deficiency diseases such as rickets, scurvy, beriberi and pellagra.
limitations: Others, including Eijkman, Funk, Stepp, and Osborne and Mendel, reached similar conclusions in the same period, so priority is shared.
Hopkins did not identify the substances themselves.

title: Salvarsan, the first 'magic bullet' drug, treats syphilis
summary: In 1909 Paul Ehrlich and Sahachiro Hata at the Georg-Speyer-Haus in Frankfurt found that an arsenic compound, number 606, cured syphilis in rabbits. Marketed in 1910 as Salvarsan, it was the first effective treatment for syphilis and a model for chemotherapy.
explanation:
Ehrlich sought chemicals that would bind to and kill microbes without harming the patient, an idea he called the 'magic bullet'. From 1906 his chemotherapy institute in Frankfurt systematically made and tested hundreds of arsenic compounds. Compound 606, arsphenamine, had been set aside as useless in 1907, but Hata, who had learned to infect rabbits with syphilis, retested it and found it highly effective.

First given to patients in spring 1909, it was reported later that year and sold as Salvarsan from 1910; some 65,000 doses had been used by the end of that year. Until then syphilis had been treated mainly with mercury. The less toxic Neosalvarsan followed, and the drugs were used until penicillin replaced them in the 1940s.

people.name: Paul Ehrlich

whyItMattered: Salvarsan showed that systematic chemical screening could produce drugs against specific microbes, a model for modern drug discovery.
limitations: Salvarsan was difficult to prepare and give and had serious side effects.
Calling it the first chemotherapy drug reflects Ehrlich's own definition; earlier remedies such as quinine and mercury had also acted against disease.

title: Mayo Clinic introduces the single patient medical record
summary: In 1907 Henry Plummer and Mabel Root at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, replaced doctors' separate ledgers with one numbered record for each patient, held centrally so that any doctor could see the patient's whole history.
explanation:
Before then, each physician at the clinic kept his own ledger, recording patients in whatever way he preferred, so information about one patient was scattered. Plummer spent more than a year studying record-keeping at other medical centres and in business before designing a system with Root in which each patient received a number and a single dossier filed in a central index.

The first patient was registered in July 1907. The system was soon adopted elsewhere and became a model for hospital medical records; by about 1935 a detailed diagnostic index had to be added as patient numbers grew.

title: The Horsley–Clarke apparatus targets deep brain structures
summary: In 1908 the surgeon Victor Horsley and the physiologist Robert Clarke in London described a frame that used three-dimensional coordinates to guide an electrode to precise points deep in an animal's brain. Their stereotaxic method became the basis of stereotactic neurosurgery.
explanation:
Horsley wanted to make small lesions in the cerebellum of monkeys and cats to study its function. Clarke applied mathematical principles: a frame fixed to the skull defined each target by distances from three planes at right angles, and an atlas of photographed brain sections gave the coordinates of each structure.

The apparatus was built in 1905 and described in the journal Brain in 1908. It was used for animal research for decades, because the position of structures in the human brain varies too much relative to the skull; stereotaxic surgery on people began only in the 1940s.

whatChanged: Points deep in the brain could be reached accurately using coordinates rather than direct sight.
whyItMattered: Stereotaxy underlies modern brain biopsy, deep brain stimulation, radiosurgery and much of experimental neuroscience.
limitations: The original frame was designed for animals and could not be used reliably in humans.
Aubrey Mussen designed a frame for humans in 1918, but stereotaxic operations on people began only in the 1940s.

title: Richter describes an intrauterine device for contraception
summary: In 1909 Richard Richter, a doctor in Waldenburg in Silesia (now Wałbrzych, Poland), reported preventing pregnancy with a ring of silkworm gut placed inside the uterus. Developed by Ernst Gräfenberg in the 1920s, intrauterine devices became one of the world's most widely used contraceptives.
explanation:
Earlier pessaries placed in the cervix often caused infection. Richter's device was a flexible ring of silkworm-gut suture with threads for removal, inserted with a notched instrument. Writing in the Deutsche Medizinische Wochenschrift, he described it as a simple, safe contraceptive that most women did not feel, and reported women who had used it for almost four years.

In the 1920s the Berlin gynaecologist Ernst Gräfenberg developed rings of silkworm gut and metal wire. Plastic IUDs followed in the 1960s, and copper was added in 1969, greatly improving their effectiveness.

whyItMattered: IUDs are now among the most widely used reversible contraceptives in the world.
limitations: Early intrauterine devices could cause infection, and later designs such as the Dalkon Shield caused serious harm.

title: Jacobaeus looks inside the human abdomen and chest
summary: In 1910 Hans Christian Jacobaeus, an internist in Stockholm, reported examining the abdominal and chest cavities of patients through a cystoscope, a technique he called laparoscopy and thoracoscopy. It was the start of minimally invasive examination of body cavities.
explanation:
In 1901 the Dresden surgeon Georg Kelling had looked into the abdomen of a dog with a cystoscope after inflating it with air. Jacobaeus, who worked on treating tuberculosis by introducing air into body cavities, applied the idea to people, at first to examine patients with fluid in the abdomen.

He published his first experience in 1910, including laparoscopy in 17 patients with ascites, and by 1912 described 97 abdominal examinations. He also used the method to look inside the chest of patients with tuberculosis, and stressed the need for special instruments and for training on animals and cadavers.

title: Malaria fever is used to treat syphilis of the brain
summary: On 14 June 1917 the Vienna psychiatrist Julius Wagner-Jauregg injected blood from a soldier with malaria into nine patients with general paresis, a fatal syphilis of the brain. The fevers halted the disease in some, and he won the 1927 Nobel Prize.
explanation:
General paresis of the insane, a late stage of syphilis, filled many asylum beds and was always fatal. Wagner-Jauregg had noticed that some psychiatric patients improved after feverish infections, and had tried tuberculin and other fever-inducing agents with little lasting success.

In 1917 he deliberately infected patients with tertian malaria, letting the fevers run before curing the malaria with quinine. Many patients improved, and malaria therapy was widely adopted in the following decades. Wagner-Jauregg became the first psychiatrist to win a Nobel Prize. Penicillin replaced the treatment in the 1940s.

whyItMattered: It was the first effective physical treatment in psychiatry and encouraged the view that mental illness could have physical causes and cures.
limitations: The treatment was never tested in a controlled trial, and its benefit is hard to judge.

title: Mellanby shows that rickets is a dietary deficiency
summary: In experiments reported in 1919, Edward Mellanby gave puppies at Cambridge diets that produced rickets, then prevented and cured the disease with fats such as cod-liver oil and butter. He concluded that rickets was caused by lack of a fat-soluble dietary factor, later named vitamin D.
explanation:
Rickets, which softens and deforms children's bones, was very common in British cities, especially in Scotland. At the suggestion of Frederick Gowland Hopkins, the Medical Research Committee asked Mellanby to investigate. In hundreds of feeding experiments with puppies, a diet based largely on oatmeal porridge produced rickets, while cod-liver oil, butter and suet were most strongly protective.

Mellanby first thought the factor was the known fat-soluble vitamin A; Elmer McCollum later showed it was a separate substance, vitamin D. Harriette Chick's team in Vienna confirmed in 1922 that cod-liver oil prevented and cured rickets in children.

title: Fidel Pagés describes lumbar epidural anaesthesia
summary: In March 1921 the Spanish military surgeon Fidel Pagés published 'Anestesia metamérica', describing the injection of local anaesthetic into the epidural space of the lower back to numb parts of the body for surgery. His work was overlooked until Achille Dogliotti described the technique again in 1931.
explanation:
Spinal anaesthesia, injecting anaesthetic into the fluid around the spinal cord, was already in use but carried risks. Pagés, a surgeon in Madrid, injected anaesthetic into the space just outside the membrane surrounding the cord, blocking nerves to particular segments of the body. He published the method in the Revista Española de Cirugía, a journal he had co-founded, and it was reprinted in the Revista de Sanidad Militar that June.

Pagés died in a road accident in 1923. In 1931 the Italian surgeon Dogliotti described the same approach, with the 'loss of resistance' technique used to find the epidural space, and was long credited as its originator.

people.name: Achille Mario Dogliotti
people.role: Italian surgeon who described the technique independently in 1931

whatChanged: Surgeons gained a way to numb a band of the body without general anaesthesia or entering the spinal fluid.
whyItMattered: Epidural anaesthesia and analgesia are now widely used for childbirth, surgery and pain relief after operations.
limitations: Pagés's paper had little influence at the time; the technique spread after Dogliotti's 1931 work.
Caudal injections into the epidural space at the base of the spine had been described earlier.
contested: Dogliotti was long credited as the originator of epidural anaesthesia; Spanish historians have argued that priority belongs to Pagés.

title: Toxoid vaccines against diphtheria and tetanus
summary: In 1923 Gaston Ramon at the Pasteur Institute's annex near Paris treated diphtheria toxin with formaldehyde and heat, making a harmless 'anatoxin' that still produced immunity. The same method gave a tetanus toxoid, tested in soldiers from 1926–27.
explanation:
Diphtheria and tetanus are caused by bacterial toxins. Antitoxin serum from horses could treat them but gave only short protection. Ramon, a veterinarian in charge of serum production at Garches, noticed that formaldehyde added to preserve sera weakened toxins; diphtheria toxin treated with formaldehyde and warmed no longer killed guinea pigs but still triggered immunity. Émile Roux presented the findings to the French Academy of Sciences on 10 December 1923.

In 1924 Pierre Descombey applied the method to tetanus toxin, and in 1926–27 Ramon and the army doctor Christian Zoeller reported vaccinating several hundred people. In London, Alexander Glenny at the Wellcome laboratories had also studied formaldehyde-treated toxin and from 1926 added aluminium salts to strengthen the response.

title: Hans Berger records the human electroencephalogram
summary: In 1924 the Jena psychiatrist Hans Berger recorded electrical activity from the human brain through the scalp. Uncertain of his results, he waited until 1929 to publish them, coining the term electroencephalogram (EEG) and describing the alpha rhythm.
explanation:
Electrical activity had been recorded from the exposed brains of animals since the late nineteenth century. Berger, working at the psychiatric clinic of the University of Jena, began recording from patients with skull defects in 1924, using a galvanometer attached to electrodes, and later from intact scalps.

His 1929 paper, 'On the electroencephalogram of man', described regular waves of about ten per second, now called alpha waves, which disappeared when the subject opened their eyes or concentrated. The work was met with scepticism until Edgar Adrian confirmed it in Cambridge in 1934.

whatChanged: The electrical activity of a living human brain could be recorded without surgery.
whyItMattered: EEG became essential for diagnosing epilepsy, studying sleep and assessing brain function.
limitations: Richard Caton and others had earlier recorded brain electricity in animals.
Early recordings were made in patients with defects in the skull, where signals were easier to pick up.

title: Whooping cough vaccines are developed and tested
summary: In the 1920s Thorvald Madsen of the Danish State Serum Institute reported that a vaccine made from whooping cough bacteria gave some protection in the Faroe Islands. In 1934–35 Pearl Kendrick and Grace Eldering in Grand Rapids, Michigan, ran a large controlled trial showing that their vaccine worked.
explanation:
Whooping cough killed more than 6,000 American children a year in the 1920s; its bacterium had been identified by Jules Bordet and Octave Gengou in 1906. Many commercial vaccines were sold, but none had been shown to work. Madsen's studies in the Faroe Islands in 1923–24 and 1929 suggested protection.

Kendrick and Eldering, at the Michigan Department of Health laboratory in Grand Rapids, began work during an outbreak in 1932. With the help of the community and local doctors they vaccinated more than 1,500 children and compared them with unvaccinated children, showing that the vaccine protected them. They helped combine the vaccine with diphtheria and tetanus toxoids into the DTP vaccine.

title: BCG, the tuberculosis vaccine, is first given to a baby
summary: On 18 July 1921, at the Charité hospital in Paris, Benjamin Weill-Hallé and Raymond Turpin gave a newborn whose mother had tuberculosis an oral dose of BCG, a weakened bovine tuberculosis bacillus developed by Albert Calmette and Camille Guérin. It remains the only licensed tuberculosis vaccine.
explanation:
At the Pasteur Institute in Lille, Calmette and Guérin spent more than a decade repeatedly culturing a bovine tuberculosis bacillus until it was too weak to cause disease. Trials in cattle were interrupted by the First World War.

The first infant, at high risk of infection at home, suffered no ill effects and lived free of tuberculosis. By the end of 1924 more than 600 infants had been vaccinated by mouth. In 1930 babies in Lübeck, Germany, died after receiving contaminated vaccine, a disaster later traced to negligence in a local laboratory. More than 4 billion doses of BCG have since been given.

limitations: Calmette and Guérin had tested the vaccine earlier in animals; the 1921 dose was the first given to a person.

BCG vaccination of babies began before rigorous trials of its effectiveness.

title: Early gender-affirming surgeries in Berlin and Dresden
summary: Between 1922 and 1931, surgeons working with Magnus Hirschfeld's Institute for Sexual Science in Berlin performed some of the first gender-affirming operations, for Dora Richter and others. The Danish painter Lili Elbe had a series of operations in Berlin and Dresden in 1930–31 and died after the last.
explanation:
Hirschfeld founded the Institute for Sexual Science in Berlin in 1919, and he and colleagues such as Ludwig Levy-Lenz, Erwin Gohrbandt and the Dresden gynaecologist Kurt Warnekros began offering surgery to trans patients. Dora Richter, who worked at the institute, had an orchidectomy in 1922 and later a vaginoplasty, and is usually regarded as the first person to complete a series of gender-affirming operations.

Lili Elbe was assessed at the institute in March 1930 and had her first operation in Berlin. Her later operations, at the Dresden Women's Clinic under Warnekros, included the transplantation of ovarian tissue and, in June 1931, an attempted uterus transplant. She died of complications in September 1931.

whyItMattered: These operations were forerunners of modern gender-affirming surgery.
limitations: Accounts differ on the number, dates and surgeons of the operations.

title: Prontosil, the first sulfonamide antibacterial drug
summary: In late 1932 Gerhard Domagk at Bayer's laboratories in Elberfeld, Germany, found that a red dye, later named Prontosil, cured mice of lethal streptococcal infections. Launched in 1935, it was the first drug that could treat a wide range of bacterial infections inside the body.
explanation:
Inspired by Paul Ehrlich's idea that dyes might attack microbes selectively, Domagk, head of experimental pathology at IG Farben's Bayer laboratories from 1927, tested azo dyes made by the company's chemists in infected mice. One, KL730, protected mice from streptococci at very low doses, although it did nothing to the bacteria in a test tube. A patent was filed on Christmas Day 1932 and the drug was tested quietly in patients before Domagk published in 1935.

In 1936 Leonard Colebrook in London reported that deaths from childbed fever fell from over 20% to 4% with Prontosil. Researchers soon found that the body breaks it down to sulfanilamide, the active part, which led to a family of cheaper sulfonamide drugs. Domagk received the 1939 Nobel Prize.

title: Insulin coma therapy for schizophrenia: adopted, then debunked
summary: In 1933 Manfred Sakel at the University of Vienna's psychiatric clinic began treating schizophrenia by giving patients enough insulin to put them into a coma, day after day for weeks. Widely adopted, the treatment was shown in the 1950s to have no specific benefit and was abandoned.
explanation:
Around 1930, working at a private clinic in Berlin, Sakel had used small doses of insulin to ease morphine withdrawal. Believing that patients' mental state improved after accidental comas, he returned to Vienna in 1933 and deliberately induced deep hypoglycaemic comas in people with schizophrenia. In 1934 he claimed full remission in 70% of patients.

The treatment spread rapidly, including to British mental hospitals, where large units treated up to 20 patients at once. Patients were put into comas five or six mornings a week for up to ten weeks. In 1953 the psychiatrist Harold Bourne argued in The Lancet that there was no evidence it worked, and a later randomised trial found no specific benefit. It fell out of use in the 1960s as antipsychotic drugs spread.

title: Convulsive therapy and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
summary: On 23 January 1934 the Hungarian psychiatrist Ladislas Meduna induced seizures with camphor in a patient with catatonia near Budapest, starting convulsive therapy. On 11 April 1938 Ugo Cerletti and Lucio Bini in Rome used electric current instead, giving the first electroconvulsive therapy.
explanation:
Meduna believed, from studying brain tissue, that epilepsy and schizophrenia were antagonistic, so that seizures might relieve psychosis. At the Lipótmező asylum outside Budapest he injected camphor oil into a man who had been in a catatonic stupor for four years; after five induced seizures he improved dramatically. Meduna then switched to pentylenetetrazol (Metrazol or Cardiazol), which produced seizures almost at once.

In Rome, Cerletti sought a simpler and more controllable way to cause seizures. On 11 April 1938 at the university's Clinic for Nervous and Mental Disorders, he and Bini passed a current through the head of a patient, starting ECT. The electrical method rapidly replaced Meduna's drugs, and Metrazol therapy was abandoned. Modern ECT is given under anaesthesia.

title: The 17D yellow fever vaccine
summary: In 1937 Max Theiler and Hugh Smith at the Rockefeller Foundation's laboratories in New York reported 17D, a strain of yellow fever virus weakened by long culture in chick embryo tissue. Tested in Brazil from 1937, the 17D vaccine is still in use, and Theiler received the 1951 Nobel Prize.
explanation:
Yellow fever kills up to half of people who develop its severe form. Earlier attempts at vaccines had failed, partly because the cause was unknown until it was shown to be a virus in the late 1920s. Theiler, who moved to the Rockefeller Foundation in 1930, found that mice could be used to study it, and in 1931 a vaccine from virus grown in mouse brains was tested, but it needed human immune serum and could cause brain inflammation.

Theiler and his colleagues then grew the Asibi strain of the virus over and over in tissue cultures, at first with mouse embryo tissue and later with chick embryo from which the brain and spinal cord had been removed. After well over 100 passages, one line, 17D, had lost its dangerous effects. Smith took it to Brazil in 1937, where vaccination began, and it was licensed in 1938.

title: Prefrontal leucotomy (lobotomy) is introduced in Lisbon
summary: On 12 November 1935 the Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz and the neurosurgeon Almeida Lima in Lisbon injected alcohol into the frontal lobes of a psychiatric patient's brain, beginning the operation of prefrontal leucotomy. Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize, but the operation caused great harm and was abandoned.
explanation:
At a neurology congress in London in August 1935, Moniz heard John Fulton and Carlyle Jacobsen describe chimpanzees that became calmer after their frontal lobes were removed. Because gout had deformed his hands, Lima carried out the operations under his direction: holes were drilled in the skull and alcohol injected to destroy frontal lobe tissue, and later a wire loop, the leucotome, was used to cut nerve fibres.

In the United States, Walter Freeman popularised the operation and developed a quick version through the eye sockets. Lobotomy was performed in many countries, mainly on people with schizophrenia, until drugs such as chlorpromazine replaced it from the mid-1950s.

date.basis: Date of the first operation; results were published in 1936, which some sources give as the date of introduction.

whatChanged: Brain surgery was used to try to treat severe mental illness.
whyItMattered: The rapid spread of lobotomy, and the harm it did, became a lasting warning about adopting drastic treatments without good evidence.
limitations: Improvements were judged without control groups.
The Nobel committee's praise reflected the lack of other treatments at the time.
harms: Lobotomy was performed on many thousands of people in many countries, often without meaningful consent, and could leave them permanently changed or disabled.
contested: Moniz's Nobel Prize remains one of the most criticised in its history, and there have been calls for it to be withdrawn.

title: Finochietto's rib spreader for chest surgery
summary: In 1936 the Argentine surgeon Enrique Finochietto of the Rawson Hospital in Buenos Aires improved the rack-and-pinion rib spreader used to hold the ribs apart in chest surgery. Retractors based on his design, such as the Burford–Finochietto, are still standard in open chest surgery.
explanation:
To operate inside the chest, surgeons must hold the ribs apart. A rack-and-pinion rib spreader with a screw lock had been introduced in 1914 by the French surgeon Théodore Tuffier.

Finochietto, chief of surgery at the Rawson Hospital and professor of surgery in Buenos Aires, modified the design in 1936. A gifted designer, he devised some 67 surgical instruments and other items. A later version, the Burford–Finochietto retractor, a robust ratchet-operated spreader with changeable blades, became one of the most familiar instruments in thoracic surgery.

whatChanged: Surgeons could open the chest more safely and keep it open steadily during long operations.
whyItMattered: Finochietto-style retractors are standard in open heart and lung surgery.
limitations: Finochietto improved an earlier design by Tuffier rather than inventing the rib spreader.

title: Kolff's artificial kidney saves its first life
summary: In 1943 Willem Kolff, a young doctor in Kampen in the occupied Netherlands, began treating kidney failure with a rotating-drum artificial kidney built from cellophane sausage casing and improvised parts. Most early patients died, but on 11 September 1945 dialysis saved Sofia Schafstadt, aged 67.
explanation:
Without working kidneys, waste builds up in the blood and causes death. Kolff wrapped about 20 metres of cellophane tubing around a slatted drum that turned in a bath of dialysing fluid; as the patient's blood flowed through the tubing, waste diffused out. The director of a local enamel factory helped build it during the German occupation.

Kolff treated his first patient in 1943, but the machine at first only improved patients' condition temporarily. Schafstadt, a prisoner held as a Nazi collaborator, regained consciousness after 11 hours of dialysis, and her kidneys recovered. After the war Kolff gave machines to hospitals in London, Montreal and New York, and later worked in the United States on artificial organs, including the artificial heart.

whatChanged: Kidney failure could be treated by cleaning the blood with a machine.
whyItMattered: Haemodialysis now keeps millions of people with kidney failure alive, and Kolff's work began the field of artificial organs.
limitations: Georg Haas had dialysed patients earlier, in Giessen in the 1920s, without lasting success.
Sources differ on whether Schafstadt was Kolff's 16th or 17th patient.

title: Nitrogen mustard begins cancer chemotherapy
summary: On 27 August 1942 at New Haven Hospital, a team led by the Yale pharmacologists Louis Goodman and Alfred Gilman gave nitrogen mustard, a chemical relative of mustard gas, to a man with advanced lymphoma known as J.D. His tumours shrank. The work, secret in wartime, was published in 1946.
explanation:
Working under a secret government contract on chemical warfare agents, Goodman and Gilman noticed that nitrogen mustard was especially toxic to lymph cells. In mice and rabbits it made lymphoma tumours shrink dramatically. With the surgeon Gustaf Lindskog they treated J.D., whose lymphosarcoma no longer responded to radiation.

His tumours regressed for a time, and further trials followed at Yale, Chicago and New York. Secrecy delayed publication until 1946. Nitrogen mustard became the model for the alkylating agents, a major class of cancer drugs still used today.

locations.name: New Haven Hospital and Yale School of Medicine

whatChanged: It showed that a drug could shrink a cancer in a person.
whyItMattered: It launched medical oncology; combination chemotherapy and many later cancer drugs build on it.
limitations: The first responses were temporary; lasting cures from chemotherapy came only later, with combinations of drugs.
The story that chemotherapy began with the 1943 Bari air raid is a myth: the Yale treatment came 15 months earlier.

title: Beck restarts a fibrillating heart with an electric shock
summary: In 1947 the Cleveland surgeon Claude Beck was closing the chest of a 14-year-old boy after an operation when the boy's heart went into ventricular fibrillation. After 45 minutes of hand massage, Beck applied an experimental defibrillator directly to the heart and restored its rhythm. The boy recovered fully.
explanation:
In ventricular fibrillation the heart quivers chaotically instead of pumping, and death follows within minutes. The boy, Richard Heyard, was being operated on at University Hospitals of Cleveland for a sunken chest. Beck reopened the chest and massaged the heart by hand while a colleague fetched a device he had been developing.

The first shock failed. Beck continued massage and then gave a second shock, which restored a normal rhythm. Beck went on to build defibrillators, taught resuscitation courses from 1950, and in 1955 his team reversed a cardiac arrest that had occurred outside the operating room.

whatChanged: A heart in fibrillation could be shocked back into a normal rhythm.
whyItMattered: Defibrillation became central to resuscitation, leading to external defibrillators and today's automated devices in public places.
limitations: Electric shocks had been used earlier to revive people, as far back as the eighteenth century.
The shock was applied to the exposed heart; shocks through the closed chest came later.

title: Paracetamol is identified as a safer painkiller
summary: In 1948 Bernard Brodie and Julius Axelrod in New York showed that the painkiller acetanilide caused a harmful blood disorder through one breakdown product, aniline, while another, N-acetyl-p-aminophenol, relieved pain without it. They suggested using it instead. It is now paracetamol, or acetaminophen.
explanation:
Popular headache remedies such as Bromo-Seltzer contained acetanilide or phenacetin, and some heavy users developed methaemoglobinaemia, in which the blood carries less oxygen. In 1946 the Institute for the Study of Analgesic and Sedative Drugs funded research into why. Axelrod, a chemist at the New York City Laboratory of Industrial Hygiene, worked with Brodie at the Goldwater Memorial Hospital research group in New York.

They developed sensitive tests for acetanilide's breakdown products in blood and urine, and found that aniline levels rose with methaemoglobin, while N-acetyl-p-aminophenol was the main product and had painkilling activity. Their 1948 paper, 'The fate of acetanilide in man', recommended it as a replacement. Paracetamol became one of the most widely used medicines in the world.

date.basis: Published in the Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics in 1948.

whatChanged: Doctors gained a painkiller and fever reducer without the blood toxicity of its parent drugs.
whyItMattered: Paracetamol is now among the most widely used medicines for pain and fever, and the work helped found the study of drug metabolism.
limitations: Paracetamol itself had been made decades earlier but had been little used.
In overdose paracetamol can cause fatal liver damage.

title: The World Health Organization is founded
summary: On 7 April 1948 the constitution of the World Health Organization came into force, after the 26th member state of the United Nations ratified it. Based in Geneva, WHO took over the work of earlier international health bodies and became the UN agency for global health.
explanation:
International cooperation on health began with the International Sanitary Conferences, the first in Paris in 1851, and continued through the Paris-based Office International d'Hygiène Publique and the League of Nations Health Organization. At the founding of the United Nations in 1945, delegates proposed a single global health body.

An International Health Conference in New York adopted WHO's constitution in June 1946, and 61 states signed it that July. It came into force on 7 April 1948, now marked each year as World Health Day, and the first World Health Assembly opened in Geneva on 24 June 1948. WHO went on to lead campaigns such as the eradication of smallpox.

whatChanged: The world gained a single permanent organisation to coordinate international health work.
whyItMattered: WHO sets international health standards, coordinates responses to epidemics and led the eradication of smallpox.
limitations: WHO depends on member states for funding and cooperation and cannot enforce its recommendations.
It built on earlier bodies, such as the Office International d'Hygiène Publique and the League of Nations Health Organization.

title: Harold Ridley implants an artificial lens in the eye
summary: On 29 November 1949 at St Thomas' Hospital, London, Harold Ridley implanted a plastic lens inside a woman's eye after removing her cataract. He chose Perspex after noticing that splinters of it from shattered aircraft canopies caused no inflammation in airmen's eyes.
explanation:
After cataract surgery, patients needed thick, heavy spectacles because the eye's own lens had been removed. During the Second World War, treating injured RAF pilots at Moorfields Eye Hospital, Ridley saw that fragments of Perspex (polymethyl methacrylate) from cockpit canopies lay in the eye without causing a reaction.

In 1948 he met privately with John Pike of the optical firm Rayner, and with John Holt of ICI, which made the plastic, to design a lens. The first operation, on a woman in her forties, was kept secret. Today the great majority of cataract operations include an intraocular lens.

whatChanged: The lens removed in cataract surgery could be replaced inside the eye, restoring sight without thick spectacles.
whyItMattered: Lens implants are now part of most of the millions of cataract operations performed every year.
limitations: Ideas for an artificial lens had been discussed earlier, but none had been implanted.
Adoption was slow; Ridley later asked whether implants had begun 'a generation too soon'.

title: Copenhagen's polio epidemic gives birth to intensive care
summary: During Copenhagen's severe polio epidemic of 1952, the anaesthetist Bjørn Ibsen showed that patients whose breathing was paralysed could be kept alive by tracheostomy and hand-squeezed positive-pressure ventilation. Students ventilated patients round the clock, and the first intensive care unit followed in 1953.
explanation:
Blegdam Hospital, the city's hospital for infectious diseases, was admitting around 50 polio patients a day, 10 to 20 of them with failing breathing, and had one tank respirator and six cuirass respirators. Nearly all patients with breathing involvement were dying. Ibsen, who had earlier kept a child with tetanus alive by sedation and hand ventilation, was called in to see Vivi Ebert, a 12-year-old who was suffocating.

He placed a tube in her windpipe through a tracheostomy and pumped air into her lungs with a rubber bag, keeping her alive. The hospital adopted the method for all such patients, with medical students taking shifts to squeeze the bags. In December 1953 the world's first intensive care unit opened at Copenhagen's Kommunehospitalet.

whatChanged: Patients who could not breathe could be kept alive for long periods with positive-pressure ventilation through the windpipe.
whyItMattered: It gave rise to intensive care medicine and modern mechanical ventilation, used for millions of patients, including during the COVID-19 pandemic.
limitations: Positive-pressure ventilation had been used earlier in anaesthesia; the advance was applying it for days or weeks to paralysed patients.
Ventilating by hand needed huge numbers of helpers; mechanical ventilators soon replaced it.

title: Nuclear transfer in frog eggs lays the basis for cloning
summary: In 1952 Robert Briggs and Thomas King at the Institute for Cancer Research in Philadelphia removed the nucleus from frog eggs and replaced it with a nucleus from a cell of an early embryo. Some of the eggs developed into tadpoles. Their nuclear transfer technique became the basis of cloning.
explanation:
Biologists wanted to know whether the nucleus of a cell loses some of its genetic potential as the cell specialises. Nuclear transplantation had been performed only in amoebae. Briggs, joined by King, who had trained in microsurgery, removed the nucleus of eggs of the leopard frog Rana pipiens and injected a nucleus taken from a blastula, an early embryo.

The eggs developed normally, showing that the technique worked. They found that nuclei from later stages supported development less well, but in 1958 John Gurdon, using a different frog, showed that nuclei from specialised cells could still direct development. Somatic cell nuclear transfer, used to clone Dolly the sheep in 1996, descends from their method.

whyItMattered: Nuclear transfer led to animal cloning and to research on stem cells and how cells become specialised.
limitations: They used nuclei from early embryos; cloning from adult cells came much later.

title: Pregnancies from frozen human sperm
summary: In 1953 Raymond Bunge and Jerome Sherman at the University of Iowa reported that three women had become pregnant with human sperm that had been frozen with glycerol, stored on dry ice and thawed. The work made sperm banks possible.
explanation:
Attempts to preserve sperm by freezing went back nearly a century, but frozen sperm rarely survived. In 1949 British scientists found that glycerol protected fowl sperm during freezing. Sherman, a zoology graduate student working in Iowa's urology department, combined glycerol with slow cooling and storage on solid carbon dioxide.

Bunge, of the university's new infertility clinic, arranged for the frozen sperm to be used in artificial insemination at the clinic. Newspaper headlines about 'fatherhood after death' brought both men heavy criticism. Freezing sperm is now routine, including for people facing cancer treatment.

title: Gibbon's heart-lung machine makes open-heart surgery possible
summary: On 6 May 1953 at Jefferson Medical College Hospital in Philadelphia, John Gibbon used a heart-lung machine he had spent two decades developing to close a hole in the heart of 18-year-old Cecelia Bavolek. It was the first successful open-heart operation with a machine taking over the work of the heart and lungs.
explanation:
In 1930, assisting the surgeon Edward Churchill in Boston, Gibbon watched a woman die from a blood clot in her lungs, and resolved to build a machine that could take over circulation and breathing during surgery. From 1934, working with his wife Mary, he developed a pump-oxygenator and tested it in animals before using it in people.

Bavolek was in heart failure from an atrial septal defect. She was supported by the machine for about 45 minutes while the hole was closed, and recovered. Gibbon's first attempt, on a 15-month-old in 1952, had failed because of a wrong diagnosis, and other early patients died. Teams elsewhere, especially at the Mayo Clinic, went on to make bypass routine.

date.basis: Date of the operation.

whatChanged: Surgeons could stop the heart and operate inside it while a machine kept the patient alive.
whyItMattered: Cardiopulmonary bypass made possible valve repair, coronary bypass, congenital heart surgery and heart transplantation.
limitations: Earlier attempts, including Gibbon's own in 1952, had failed.
Other surgeons, using cross-circulation and later improved machines, contributed as much to making open-heart surgery routine.

title: Edler and Hertz record the heart with ultrasound
summary: On 29 October 1953 in Lund, Sweden, the cardiologist Inge Edler and the physicist Hellmuth Hertz recorded echoes from a beating heart with an ultrasound device lent by Siemens. Their technique, echocardiography, became a basic tool of cardiology.
explanation:
Edler, head of cardiology at Lund's University Hospital, was responsible for assessing patients before heart surgery and wanted a better way to judge narrowing of the mitral valve. Hertz, a physics graduate student whose father, the Nobel laureate Gustav Hertz, had directed a Siemens research laboratory, knew that industrial 'reflectoscopes' used ultrasound echoes to find flaws in metal.

In May 1953 they borrowed a device for a weekend and saw echoes moving with the heartbeat. Siemens then lent them a reflectoscope, which arrived in October 1953 and was never returned. Hertz rigged a camera to record the oscilloscope trace, and they published in 1954. They later used ultrasound to diagnose fluid around the heart and a heart tumour.

date.basis: Date of the first recording, published in 1954.

whatChanged: The moving structures of the heart could be seen without surgery, catheters or X-rays.
whyItMattered: Echocardiography is now used routinely to diagnose heart valve disease, heart failure and congenital heart defects.
limitations: Others had experimented earlier with ultrasound in medicine, though Edler and Hertz said they were unaware of that work.
The first recordings showed only lines on a screen; two-dimensional images came later.

title: The first successful kidney transplant, between identical twins
summary: On 23 December 1954 at the Peter Bent Brigham Hospital in Boston, surgeons transplanted a kidney from Ronald Herrick into his identical twin Richard, who was dying of kidney failure. Because the twins were genetically identical, the kidney was not rejected. It was the first lastingly successful organ transplant.
explanation:
Kidneys transplanted between unrelated people had always been rejected by the recipient's immune system. When Richard Herrick, aged 23, was referred to the hospital, his doctors realised that an identical twin's kidney might be accepted. The team confirmed that the brothers were identical, including by comparing fingerprints at a police station, despite criticism of operating on a healthy donor.

J. Hartwell Harrison removed a kidney from Ronald, and Joseph Murray attached it in Richard, in a five-and-a-half-hour operation; the nephrologist John Merrill had used dialysis to stabilise Richard beforehand. Richard returned to an active life, and Ronald suffered no ill effects. Murray shared the 1990 Nobel Prize.

whyItMattered: It opened the era of organ transplantation; with anti-rejection drugs, kidney transplants between unrelated people followed in the early 1960s.
limitations: A temporary, partial kidney transplant had been carried out earlier at the same hospital, in 1946.
The method worked only between identical twins until immunosuppressive drugs were developed.

title: Malmström's vacuum extractor for assisted birth
summary: In 1953–54 the Swedish obstetrician Tage Malmström described a practical vacuum extractor: a metal cup held to the baby's head by suction, with a chain through which the doctor could pull during a difficult birth. It became a widely used alternative to forceps.
explanation:
James Young Simpson had tried a suction 'air tractor' in Edinburgh in 1849 but abandoned it for forceps. Malmström's cup was a hollow metal hemisphere; suction drew the baby's scalp into it, forming a swelling that held it firmly, and a hand pump created the vacuum. Unlike earlier suction cups, it was designed to transmit traction.

He described it in a Swedish journal in 1953 and in Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica in 1954, with a fuller account in 1957. Use spread rapidly in Europe, though American doctors were more cautious about risks to the baby. Later soft and disposable cups developed from his design, and vacuum delivery causes less injury to the mother's pelvic floor than forceps.

limitations: An earlier suction device by James Young Simpson in 1849 had been abandoned.

title: Tetracycline, an antibiotic improved by chemistry
summary: In 1952 Lloyd Conover, a chemist at Pfizer, made tetracycline by replacing a chlorine atom in the natural antibiotic Aureomycin with hydrogen. It soon became the most prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotic in the United States, and showed that natural antibiotics could be improved by chemistry.
explanation:
The first tetracycline antibiotics, discovered as natural products of soil bacteria, were reported in 1948: Aureomycin (chlortetracycline), found by Benjamin Duggar's soil-screening team at Lederle, and Terramycin (oxytetracycline), found by Pfizer. Conover joined a Pfizer team that, with the Harvard chemist R. B. Woodward, worked out the structures of these molecules.

Realising that the molecules could be altered, Conover removed the chlorine from Aureomycin by catalytic reduction. The product, tetracycline, was more potent and went on sale in 1953. It was used against many infections, including pneumonia and gonorrhoea, and the approach of modifying natural antibiotics became standard in the industry.
